clinicalPearls: Pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas (PPGLs) are catecholamine-producing tumors arising from sympathetic (adrenal medulla, sympathetic trunk) or parasympathetic (carotid body, glomus tympanicum/jugulare/vagale) paraganglia; by WHO usage pheochromocytoma denotes the adrenal tumor and paraganglioma denotes tumors at all other sites.

The classic triad is episodic palpitations, headache, and profuse sweating, present in roughly one-third of patients; the combination of this triad with hypertension makes pheochromocytoma a likely diagnosis, though tumors can remain asymptomatic for years.
Hypertension is the dominant sign and may be paroxysmal (classic) or sustained (also common); paroxysms generally last under one hour.
The classic 'rule of tens' states that about 10% are bilateral, 10% extra-adrenal, and 10% metastatic.
Diagnosis rests on two equally important pillars: biochemical documentation of catecholamine excess and imaging localization of the tumor.

Plasma free metanephrines are the most sensitive biochemical test and are less prone to false-positive elevation from stress including venipuncture; most tumors continuously leak O-methylated metabolites even when catecholamine secretion fluctuates.

Values three times the upper limit of normal make the diagnosis highly likely regardless of assay; because the tumor is rare, borderline elevations are more likely to be false positives, so drug/dietary confounders should be excluded and testing repeated.
On unenhanced CT, an adrenal mass with attenuation below 10 Hounsfield units makes pheochromocytoma unlikely; about 5% of adrenal incidentalomas prove to be pheochromocytomas on endocrine evaluation.

Histology classically shows a 'Zellballen' pattern of neuroendocrine chief cell nests with peripheral sustentacular cells; chief cells stain for chromogranin and synaptophysin, sustentacular cells for S-100, and loss of SDHB staining suggests an underlying germline SDH mutation.
About 25-33% of patients have an inherited syndrome (MEN 2, VHL, NF1, paraganglioma syndromes, TMEM127, MAX); these patients present on average about 15 years younger than those with sporadic tumors.

Universal germline panel testing is the gold standard and identifies a genetic cause in up to about 30% of cases, with higher yield in early onset, extra-adrenal, multiple, or metastatic tumors or a family history.
Pheochromocytoma in pregnancy may produce adrenergic crises, possibly via hCG/LHCG-receptor-mediated stimulation of epinephrine production, and is challenging to manage.
harrison.pathophysiology: PPGLs are well-vascularized neuroendocrine tumors derived from chromaffin cells of the sympathetic and parasympathetic paraganglial system. They synthesize and store catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine), and tumoral release drives the clinical syndrome; the name pheochromocytoma reflects the dark staining produced by chromaffin oxidation of catecholamines. The etiology of sporadic tumors is unknown, but 25-33% carry germline mutations. Susceptibility genes fall into three pathogenetic clusters: cluster 1 (pseudohypoxia: SDHx, FH, VHL, HIF2A), cluster 2 (kinase signaling: RET, NF1, TMEM127, MAX, HRAS, KIF1B-beta, PDH), and cluster 3 (Wnt signaling: CSDE1, MAML3). Most genes act as tumor suppressors with biallelic inactivation, while RET is a protooncogene whose mutations activate receptor tyrosine kinase activity; SDH is a Krebs-cycle/mitochondrial respiratory chain enzyme, and the VHL protein is part of a ubiquitin E3 ligase whose loss upregulates cell-cycle, glucose metabolism, and oxygen-sensing pathways.
additionalDifferentials: Anxiety/panic attacks (may be mistaken for psychiatric illness)
Mastocytosis or carcinoid syndrome (usually without hypertension)
For an asymptomatic adrenal mass: nonfunctioning adrenal adenoma, aldosteronoma, cortisol-producing adenoma (Cushing's syndrome)
additionalInvestigations: 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines (high sensitivity for initial screening)
Plasma free metanephrines (most sensitive, least stress-confounded)
Contrast CT or T2-weighted MRI with gadolinium for localization (MRI somewhat better for extra-adrenal disease)
Functional imaging: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT and 18F-DOPA PET/CT (very high sensitivity and specificity, >95%)
123I/131I-MIBG scintigraphy and 18F-FDG PET, useful in hereditary and metastatic disease
Immunohistochemistry (chromogranin, synaptophysin, S-100, SDHB) on resected tissue
Postoperative documentation of catecholamine normalization and ACTH stimulation test after bilateral cortex-sparing surgery
redFlags: Catecholamine crisis causing heart failure, pulmonary edema, arrhythmias, or intracranial hemorrhage
Paroxysms precipitated by surgery, anesthesia/intubation, positional change, exercise, micturition (bladder paraganglioma), pregnancy, or drugs (tricyclics, opiates, metoclopramide)
Paradoxical hypertensive response to antihypertensive drugs
Beta blockade given before adequate alpha blockade (risk of worsened hypertension)
Hypertensive crisis or adrenergic crisis during pregnancy
Features suggesting a hereditary syndrome (early onset, bilateral/multifocal, extra-adrenal, family history, MTC, retinal/CNS/renal tumors)
harrison.prognosis: Complete tumor removal is potentially curative and can prevent lethal hypertensive crises. About 5-10% of PPGLs are metastatic; histologic criteria alone are insufficient to define malignancy, and the WHO now uses 'metastatic' (lymph node or distant spread, commonly to lung, bone, or liver) rather than 'malignant.' The prognosis of metastatic disease is variable with 5-year survival of roughly 30-60%. Hereditary syndromes influence risk: about one-third of PGL4 (SDHB) patients develop metastases, the highest rate among the associated syndromes, and metastatic disease also occurs notably with VHL, NF1, and PGL1.
pitfalls: Borderline biochemical elevations are frequently false positives given tumor rarity; failing to exclude dietary/drug confounders (sympathomimetics, diuretics, tricyclics, alpha/beta blockers, levodopa withdrawal) and repeat testing leads to overdiagnosis.
Serial catecholamine levels vary widely due to fluctuating secretion, so reliance on a single catecholamine measurement can miss the diagnosis; metanephrines are continuously leaked.
Starting a beta blocker before adequate alpha blockade can precipitate severe hypertension.
FNA of a presumed adrenal mass that is actually a pheochromocytoma can provoke a crisis.
Standard histologic atypia, mitoses, and local invasion do not reliably establish malignancy.
Symptoms can be misattributed to a primary psychiatric/panic disorder.
NF1 germline mutations are essentially never found in sporadic pheochromocytoma, so NF1 testing is unnecessary without other neurofibromatosis features.
Sequencing protocols may miss large single- or multi-exon deletions.
harrison.severityClassification: Malignancy/recurrence risk is assessed by markers including tumor size >5 cm, the Pheochromocytoma of the Adrenal gland Scaled Score (PASS), the Grading system for Adrenal Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma (GAPP), and SDHB status, although these remain controversial. Disease is now categorized by the WHO as localized versus metastatic (regional lymph node or distant metastasis) rather than benign versus malignant.
